objectives.outcome: You can predict a poem's content from its title and test the prediction against the text.
objectives.by_the_end: By the end you can answer a short-response question naming the poem's main theme with textual evidence.

items.text: You can say whether your prediction matched the text, and explain why.
You can state the poem's main theme using evidence from specific lines.

items.q: Look only at the title 'Travel' on the board. Before we read a word, tell your partner: what do you think this poem will be about?
items.a: Any reasonable guess — journeys, foreign places, adventure. The point is that pupils commit to a prediction before reading.

items.q: Name one landmark you would like to visit and say which country it is in.
items.a: Any correct landmark-country pairing, e.g. the Eiffel Tower, France.

items.q: In our last reading, what clue in the text told you what the passage was mainly about?
items.a: Pupils recall using the title, opening lines or repeated key words as clues — from the previous chapter's reading.

blocks.question: You have guessed what 'Travel' will be about from its title alone. The poet never actually leaves his chair in this poem — so how can it still be about travel?
blocks.look_for: Pupils notice the poem is about imagined or wished-for travel, not a real journey — a prediction they can only confirm by reading closely.

items.meaning: the main idea an author explores in a piece of writing
a guess about what a text will contain, made before or while reading

blocks.text: Pupils often confuse the poem's SETTING (far-off places) with its THEME (the longing to travel). Push them past 'it's about deserts and jungles' to 'it's about wanting to travel'.
The poet stays in one place and imagines journeys he has not taken — so this poem is about the WISH to travel, built entirely from pictures in his head. Let's test that against the text itself.

items: The poem 'Travel' is by Robert Louis Stevenson, a Scottish novelist, essayist, poet and travel writer (p.118).
Lines 1-2 state the poem's wish directly: 'I should like to rise and go / Where the golden apples grow'.
The rest of the poem lists imagined places: parrot islands, Eastern cities, the Great Wall, hot forests.
A prediction made from a title is tested, then accepted or revised, by reading the actual lines.

blocks.title: I do — p.117, lines 1-2
blocks.prompt: Read the opening two lines: 'I should like to rise and go / Where the golden apples grow'. What does this tell us about the poem's theme, and does it match our prediction from the title?
steps: 'I should like to' signals a WISH, not something already happening.
'Golden apples' is an imagined, almost fairy-tale place — not a real destination.
So the theme is the LONGING to travel to faraway, wonderful places.
Compare this to the prediction on the board: if someone guessed 'adventure' or 'far-off places', the text confirms it; if someone guessed something unrelated, we now revise it.
blocks.result: Theme so far: a wish to travel to distant, wonderful places — confirmed by the poem's own opening lines.

blocks.text: A pupil may say the theme is 'deserts and jungles' because those words appear often. Redirect: those are PLACES mentioned, not the THEME — ask 'why does the poet mention them?' to reach 'because he wishes he could see them'.

blocks.title: We do — together on the board, p.117-118
blocks.prompt: Read the lines about the Great Wall and the hot forests together: 'Where the Great Wall round China goes... Where are forests, hot as fire, / Wide as England, tall as a spire'. What do these lines ADD to our theme?
steps: These are two more imagined places — China and a vast tropical forest.
Notice the poet compares them to things he knows: 'Wide as England' — he imagines the unfamiliar using the familiar.
You fill this in: does this line change our theme, or confirm it?
blocks.answer: It confirms the theme — the poem keeps listing distant places the poet wishes to see, each described through imagination and comparison.

items.q: Name two places mentioned in the poem that the poet imagines visiting.
items.a: Any two of: parrot islands, Eastern cities, China/the Great Wall, hot forests, the Nile, jungles, a deserted desert city. (Accept any two named places from the poem.)

items.q: What do you think is the main theme of this poem? (p.117, While-Reading Question)
items.a: The theme is the poet's longing or wish to travel to distant, wonderful, imagined places — shown by the repeated 'Where...' structure and the opening 'I should like to rise and go'.

items.q: Was your prediction from the warm-up acceptable, or should it be modified? Explain using one line from the poem.
items.a: Pupils compare their own prediction to the confirmed theme (longing to travel) and explain using a quoted line, e.g. 'I should like to rise and go' shows it is a wish, not a real journey — so a prediction of 'an adventure story' would need modifying to 'a poem about imagining travel'.

checkpoint.question: Explain whether your prediction about the poem's content was acceptable or needed to be modified, using evidence from the text.
mark_scheme: 2 marks: + names the actual theme (wish to travel to imagined places)
4 marks: + explains match/mismatch using a quoted line as evidence

exit_ticket.q: In one sentence, what is the theme of 'Travel'?
exit_ticket.a: The poet's wish/longing to travel to distant, imagined places.

exit_ticket.q: Quote one line from the poem and explain how it shows this is an imagined journey, not a real one.
exit_ticket.a: Any line beginning 'I should like to rise and go' or similar — accept any correctly quoted line showing wish/imagination, with a brief explanation linking it to longing rather than an actual trip.

sections.reteach_rule: If more than a third of the class state the theme as a list of places rather than the WISH to travel, redo the I-do on lines 1-2 before moving to vocabulary work next period.

homework_key.answer: (B) He is imagining places he wishes to visit — the poem opens 'I should like to rise and go', a wish, not an account of an actual journey.
(B) 'I should like to rise and go' — this is the line that most directly states the poet's longing to travel.

Open response. A strong answer states a clear prediction (e.g. 'I predicted an adventure story'), says whether it matched (e.g. 'it needed modifying'), and explains using a quoted line (e.g. 'I should like to rise and go' shows it is about wishing to travel, not an adventure that actually happens).

one_screen:
*Objective* Pupils predict what the poem 'Travel' is about from its title, then test that prediction against the actual lines, and state the poem's theme with evidence.

*Warm-up* Before reading, pupils guess what 'Travel' will be about from the title alone and say their guess to a partner — no peeking at the text yet.

*Worked example* Read lines 1-2 together: 'I should like to rise and go / Where the golden apples grow'. Show pupils that 'should like to' signals a WISH, not a real journey — so the theme is longing to travel, not an actual adventure.

*Practice* Pupils name two imagined places from the poem, then answer the book's own While-Reading question on the main theme, then explain whether their own earlier prediction needs modifying, quoting one line as proof.

*Misconception* Watch for pupils naming the THEME as a list of places (deserts, China, jungles) instead of the WISH behind them — ask 'why does he mention these?' to pull them back to longing/imagination.

*Exit* Pupils write the poem's theme in one sentence and quote one line that proves it is an imagined journey, not a real one.
